definitions.text: Divisions formed by bulkheads and decks constructed of steel or equivalent material, stiffened, and insulated with approved non-combustible materials such that the average unexposed face temperature rise does not exceed 140°C above original temperature, nor single point 180°C, within the specified time (A-60: 60 min, A-30: 30 min, A-15: 15 min, A-0: 0 min), and capable of preventing passage of smoke and flame for 60 minutes.
The government of the State whose flag the ship is entitled to fly.

The government of the State whose flag the ship is entitled to fly — identical wording to SOLAS's own definition, which the FSS Code cross-references directly rather than restating independently in substance.

One of Part C's defined navigation-light terms — COLREG Rule 21 (Definitions) establishes all-round light as a light showing an unbroken arc over 360 degrees of the horizon. This repository's decomposition captures the term at Rule 21 level; the regulation's own further detail is not yet broken out to paragraph-level nodes.
A protective suit designed for use by rescue boat crews and marine evacuation system parties which reduces thermal shock upon immersion and provides adequate insulation during rescue operations.

SOLAS Chapter XIII, Regulation 1 defines Audit as a systematic, independent, documented process for obtaining and objectively evaluating audit evidence against audit criteria; Audit Scheme as the IMO Member State Audit Scheme itself; Code for Implementation as the III Code (resolution A.1070(28)); and Audit Standard as the Code for Implementation.

Divisions formed by bulkheads, decks, ceilings or linings constructed of approved non-combustible materials capable of preventing the passage of flame for 30 minutes, with insulation value such that the average unexposed face temperature rise does not exceed 140°C above original temperature, nor single point 180°C, within the specified time (B-15: 15 min, B-0: 0 min).
A ship intended primarily to carry dry cargo in bulk, including such types as ore carriers and combination carriers.

A dedicated space or open deck area on board ship containing bunkering manifolds, isolation valves, emergency release couplings, drip trays, and safety connections for transferring low-flashpoint fuel.
The transfer of liquid or gaseous fuel from land-based or floating facilities into a ship's permanent tanks, or the connection of portable tanks to the ship's fuel supply system.

A person who holds a certificate of proficiency in survival craft and rescue boats issued under the authority of, or recognized as valid by, the Administration in accordance with the requirements of the STCW Convention.

The owner of the ship or any other organization or person such as the manager or bareboat charterer who has assumed responsibility for operation from the owner and agreed to take over all ISM Code duties.

A switchboard which in the event of failure of the main electrical power supply system is directly supplied by the emergency source of electrical power or the transitional source of emergency electrical power and intended to distribute electrical energy to the emergency services.

As defined by the Tonnage Convention 1969 (Regulation 2, Definitions), the terms that fix which spaces count toward a ship's total moulded volume V for tonnage-measurement purposes — including which spaces count as 'enclosed' and the concept of a weathertight boundary that determines whether a space counts as enclosed. Distinct from the unrelated 'enclosed space entry' safety concept (confined-space hazard procedures) used elsewhere in maritime regulation — this term is specific to tonnage volume measurement.

The satellite service operating on 406 MHz that SOLAS Chapter IV, Regulation 3 defines as one of the GMDSS distress-alerting terms — the frequency band on which an EPIRB (Emergency Position-Indicating Radio Beacon) transmits.

A machinery space designed to serve as non-hazardous under normal operating conditions, but provided with emergency shutdown arrangements that automatically isolate non-certified electrical equipment and gas supply upon gas detection.
A group of fire detectors and manual call points served by a single section indicator on the main fire alarm panel.
A fixed fire-extinguishing installation capable of producing and distributing foam to protect machinery spaces or deck cargo areas.

One of Part C's defined navigation-light terms — COLREG Rule 21 (Definitions) establishes flashing light as a light flashing at regular intervals at a specified frequency. This repository's decomposition captures the term at Rule 21 level; the regulation's own frequency detail is not yet broken out to paragraph-level nodes.

The lowest temperature at which a liquid gives off vapour in sufficient concentration to form an ignitable mixture with air, as used as one of the defined terms in MSC.1/Circ.1321's engine-room and cargo pump-room fire-prevention guidelines, alongside auto-ignition point, potential ignition sources, and flammable oils.

FSS Code Chapter 6 (Fixed fire-extinguishing systems — Foam) defines the terminology its foam systems depend on: foam concentrate (the raw fire-fighting foam agent), foam solution (concentrate mixed with water in the design mixing ratio), the foam mixing ratio itself, foam delivery ducts, design filling rate, nominal flow rate, application rate, foam expansion ratio, foam production, filling rate and filling time.

Normally the uppermost complete deck exposed to weather and sea, fitted with permanent means of closing every opening in its weather part, with watertight closing means for all openings below it in the ship's sides; on a cargo ship the freeboard deck may be taken as the bulkhead deck.
A space containing pumps, compressors and/or vaporizers for fuel preparation and conditioning, provided with dedicated mechanical extraction ventilation maintaining negative pressure.

As defined by FSS Code Chapter 15: gas-free describes a space where the hydrocarbon/flammable vapour concentration is below 1% of the lower flammable limit (LFL) and the oxygen content is at least 21%, with no toxic gases present; gas-safe describes a space that is safe, in terms of its gas content, for a stated purpose or activity.
Natural gas or other hydrocarbon fuel having a flashpoint below 60°C, carried or used on board ships for propulsion or auxiliary energy generation.

term: Global Maritime Distress and Safety System (GMDSS)

definitions.text: The worldwide integrated radio communications network established under SOLAS Chapter IV, incorporating terrestrial and satellite systems for distress alerting and maritime safety information.
The measure of the overall size of a ship determined in accordance with the provisions of Regulation 3 of Annex I of the 1969 Tonnage Convention.

An area in which an explosive gas atmosphere is or may be expected to be present, in quantities requiring special precautions for the construction, installation, and use of equipment. Classified into Zone 0, Zone 1, and Zone 2 based on frequency and duration of explosive atmosphere presence.
A fixed fire-extinguishing system using foam generators (of the inside-air or outside-air type) to produce high-expansion foam, as defined and specified in FSS Code Chapter 6.

MSC.1/Circ.1321 (Guidelines for Measures to Prevent Fires in Engine-Rooms and Cargo Pump-Rooms) distinguishes a high temperature surface — above 220 degrees C — from a hot surface — below 220 degrees C, a category that includes steam systems operating under 2.3 N/mm2, thermal oil systems, exhaust gas piping, and oil-fired or exhaust-gas boilers.
Any uninsulated surface in an engine room or boiler space having a temperature exceeding 220°C, capable of igniting fuel or oil spray.
Surfaces with temperatures exceeding 220°C which may be impinged as a result of a fuel system failure shall be properly insulated.
Any occurrence, or series of occurrences having the same origin, which causes pollution damage or creates a grave and imminent threat of causing such damage, as defined by CLC 1992 Article I.
An inert gas plant and inert gas distribution system designed to maintain an atmosphere in cargo tanks with an oxygen content of not more than 5% by volume.
A rigid survival craft capable of sustaining and protecting occupants during abandonment at sea, complying with LSA Code Section 4.4.

The lowest concentration of a flammable vapour or gas in air at which ignition can occur, defined as one of MSC.1/Circ.1321's terms; also used as the reference threshold in FSS Code Chapter 15's own 'gas-free' definition (below 1% LFL).

A conversion of an existing ship is treated as a 'major conversion' if it substantially alters the ship's dimensions or carrying capacity, changes the ship's type, is intended (in the Administration's view) to substantially prolong the ship's life, or otherwise alters the ship so much that — had it been built new in that form — provisions of MARPOL not applicable to it as an existing ship would now apply. The practical effect is that a major-conversion ship is generally held to new-ship construction/equipment standards rather than the lighter existing-ship standards.

SOLAS does not use the identical defined term, but Chapter II-1 Regulation 1 (Application) reaches the same practical result through different wording: repairs, alterations and modifications 'of a major character' (and outfitting related to them) must meet the requirements for a new ship, so far as the Administration considers reasonable and practicable. Related concept, not an identically-worded definition — flagged here deliberately rather than presented as a matching quote.

definitions.instrument: MARPOL Annex VI (2021 Revised, per MEPC.328(76))
definitions.text: Annex VI defines 'major conversion' using the same four general limbs as Annex I (substantially altering dimensions/carrying capacity/engine power; changing ship type; substantially prolonging the ship's life in the Administration's opinion; or otherwise making the ship subject to new-ship provisions it would not otherwise meet) plus a fifth limb unique to this Annex: a conversion that substantially alters the ship's energy efficiency and includes any modification that could cause the ship to exceed its applicable required EEDI (Reg. 24) or required EEXI (Reg. 25). This fifth limb is the genuinely distinct addition the 2021 revision made to the term.

One of the GMDSS-related terms defined by SOLAS Chapter IV, Regulation 3, alongside SART, recognized mobile satellite service, the 406 MHz EPIRB satellite service, and the A1-A3 sea-area classification that together determine a ship's required radiocommunications equipment. This repository's decomposition captures MSI at chapter/regulation level; its own detailed content is not yet broken out to paragraph level.

A white light placed over the fore and aft centerline of the vessel showing an unbroken light over an arc of the horizon of 225 degrees and so fixed as to show the light from right ahead to 22.5 degrees abaft the beam on either side.

A material which neither burns nor gives off flammable vapours in sufficient quantity for self-ignition when heated to approximately 750°C, as determined by the non-combustibility test specified in Part 1 of Annex 1 to the 2010 FTP Code.
Persistent hydrocarbon mineral oil, such as crude oil and fuel oil, as defined by CLC 1992 Article I.

The person designated to coordinate search and rescue operations within a specified area, as defined by SAR Convention 1979 Chapter 1.1 — the role that keeps multiple assisting units and services working to the same plan at the scene of a distress.

The person or persons registered as the owner of the ship, or, in the absence of registration, the person or persons owning the ship, as defined by CLC 1992 Article I — the 'registered owner' standard the Convention channels strict liability to.
Machinery spaces provided with automated control, alarm, and fire protection systems approved by the Administration to permit safe operation without continuous engine-room watchkeeping.
Loss or damage caused outside the ship by contamination resulting from the escape or discharge of oil from the ship, wherever such escape or discharge may occur.

Any discharge into the sea of oil or oily mixture from ships of 400 GT and above is prohibited except when en route, processed through 15 ppm oil filtering equipment, and not originating from cargo pump-room bilges on oil tankers.

term: Position 1 and Position 2 (Closing Appliance Exposure Zones)

definitions.text: Position 1 comprises exposed freeboard and raised quarter decks over their entire length, plus exposed superstructure decks forward of 0.25L from the forward perpendicular. Position 2 comprises exposed superstructure decks aft of 0.25L from the forward perpendicular at or above one standard superstructure height above the freeboard deck, and exposed superstructure decks forward of 0.25L from the forward perpendicular at or above two standard superstructure heights above the freeboard deck. These zones grade how strictly hatch, door and opening closing appliances must resist weather exposure elsewhere in the Rules.
A satellite communication service recognized under SOLAS Chapter IV for GMDSS purposes — its coverage is what defines Sea Area A3 under the Chapter's own sea-area classification.

The unit responsible for promoting efficient organization of search and rescue services and for coordinating the conduct of search and rescue operations within a search and rescue region, as defined by SAR Convention 1979 Chapter 1.1.

A unit subordinate to a rescue co-ordination centre, established to complement it within a specified area of a search and rescue region according to particular provisions of the responsible authorities, as defined by SAR Convention 1979 Chapter 1.1.
A unit composed of trained personnel and equipped with facilities suitable for the prompt conduct of search and rescue operations, as defined by SAR Convention 1979 Chapter 1.1.
A 9.2-9.5 GHz radar search and rescue transponder, defined in SOLAS Chapter IV, Regulation 3 as one of the GMDSS equipment terms driving the radiocommunications carriage requirements of Chapter IV.

SOLAS Chapter IV, Regulation 3 defines the sea-area classification that drives GMDSS equipment carriage scales: Sea Area A1 is within VHF DSC (digital selective calling) coverage; Sea Area A2 is within MF DSC coverage; Sea Area A3 is within recognized mobile satellite service coverage, beyond A1/A2.

A defined area of specified dimensions, associated with a rescue co-ordination centre, within which search and rescue services are provided, as defined by SAR Convention 1979 Chapter 1.1 (Definitions) — the term that lets a distress case, a tasking instruction, or a hand-over between two Parties' services refer unambiguously to the same area.

As defined by CLC 1992 Article I, a seagoing vessel of any type whatsoever constructed or adapted to carry oil in bulk as cargo — the definition that fixes which vessels the Convention's civil-liability regime for oil pollution damage applies to.

SOLAS Chapter XII distinguishes single-side-skin construction — any cargo hold bounded by the side shell, or by a double-skin arrangement narrower than 760mm (or 1,000mm, depending on the ship's build date) — from double-side-skin construction, where every cargo hold is bounded by a double skin formed by a longitudinal bulkhead connecting the double bottom to the deck.

One of Part C's defined navigation-light terms — COLREG Rule 21 (Definitions) establishes sidelights (a vessel's port and starboard navigation lights) with their own required arcs of visibility and colours. This repository's decomposition captures the term at Rule 21 level; the specific arc-of-visibility/colour figures are not yet broken out to their own paragraph-level nodes.
The machinery, rudder actuators, steering gear power units and ancillary equipment necessary for applying torque to the rudder stock for steering the ship.

One of Part C's defined navigation-light terms — COLREG Rule 21 (Definitions) establishes sternlight with its own required arc of visibility and colour. This repository's decomposition captures the term at Rule 21 level; the specific arc-of-visibility/colour figures are not yet broken out to their own paragraph-level nodes.

The characteristic of a material surface describing its resistance to the propagation of flame under radiant heat exposure, evaluated by measuring Critical Flux at Extinguishment (CFE ≥ 20 kW/m²), Heat for Sustained Burning (Qsb ≥ 1.5 MJ/m²), and Peak Heat Release Rate (qp ≤ 4.0 kW) per Part 5 of Annex 1 to the 2010 FTP Code.

One of Part C's defined navigation-light terms — COLREG Rule 21 (Definitions) establishes towing light with its own required arc of visibility and colour, used by vessels engaged in towing. This repository's decomposition captures the term at Rule 21 level; the specific arc-of-visibility/colour figures are not yet broken out to their own paragraph-level nodes.

A Type A ship is one designed to carry only liquid cargoes in bulk, with high exposed-deck integrity (small, gasketed steel-cover access openings only) and low permeability of loaded cargo compartments, assigned freeboard under the International Convention on Load Lines; every ship not meeting the Type A definition is a Type B ship, also freeboarded under the ICLL. Type B-60 and Type B-100 are Type B ships over 100m long permitted, under applicable ICLL requirements, a tabular freeboard reduced by up to 60% or 100% respectively of the difference between the B and A tabular values; Type B+ denotes a cargo ship carrying increased freeboard on account of its hatch cover arrangement.
The systematic audit of a Contracting Government by the IMO to verify enforcement of mandatory IMO conventions.

A closing appliance is watertight if it is designed to prevent the passage of water in either direction under a head of water for which the surrounding structure is designed; generally, all openings below the freeboard deck in the outer hull or main watertight bulkheads must have permanent means of watertight closing.

A closing appliance is weathertight if it is designed to prevent the passage of water into the ship in any sea condition; generally, all openings on the freeboard deck and in enclosed superstructures must be fitted with weathertight closing appliances.
